scenes.narration: This is one of the most important ideas in Python, and it explains many strange bugs. Today we learn what copying really means.

scenes.onScreen: "One list, two names": three numbered lines (1. b = a gives a second name to the same list; 2. copy() or a[:] makes a new list; 3. is checks if two names point to the same object) and an analogy card: one house with two name boards: a visitor who repaints the house changes it for both names

scenes.narration: When you write b equals a, Python does not copy the list. It ties a second name to the same list. Think of one house with two name boards. A visitor who repaints the house changes it for both names. To make a real copy, call the copy method, or take a slice of everything. The is operator asks, are these two names tied to the very same object?

code.source:

scenes.narration: Here is the picture, and it is the most important one in this module. Two name tags, a and b, and two arrows that point at one list object. There is one list, holding one, two, three, four. Both names lead to it. That is why a change through b shows up in a. Remember this picture whenever lists behave oddly.

scenes.onScreen: copy_demo.py: copy() and a slice both make a new list
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 1] The original list. [HL 2] The copy method makes a brand new list with the same items. [HL 3] A slice with no start and no stop does the same job. [HL 4] Now we append four to b only. [HL 5] The original and c are untouched. Only b has the four. [HL 6] And is gives False. These are three separate lists.

code.source:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a.copy()
c = a[:]
b.append(4)
print(a, b, c)
print(a is b)

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: b equals a is not a copy
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We wanted a copy, so we could change b and keep a safe. But a changed too. Because b equals a is not a copy. It is a second name for the same list. Call the copy method instead, and b becomes its own list. Now a stays exactly as it was.

props.why: b = a only gives the same list a second name, so changing b changes a; use a.copy() to get an independent list.

shorts.title: b equals a
shorts.hook: "When you write b equals a, and a is a list, Python does not copy the list."
shorts.script: When you write b equals a, and a is a list, Python does not copy the list. It gives the same list a second name. There is still only one list. Think of one house with two name boards. If someone repaints the house, both names show the new colour. This one idea explains a very large share of strange bugs in Python programs. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Not a copy.

shorts.title: Two names, one list
shorts.script: Here is the proof. A is a list of one, two, three. B equals a. Append four through b. Now print a, and it shows four as well. The is operator says True. A and b are two arrows pointing to one list. Anything you change through one name shows through the other. It is not a bug, it is how names work. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: One object, two names.

shorts.title: A real copy
shorts.hook: "To make a real copy of a list, call its copy method."
shorts.script: To make a real copy of a list, call its copy method. B equals a dot copy. Or take a slice of everything, a bracket colon bracket. Either way, Python builds a brand new list with the same items. Now a and b are independent. Changing b does not touch a. Use copy whenever you need to change a list and keep the original safe. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Make it independent.

shorts.title: The shared list bug
shorts.script: A classic bug. You want a safe copy, so you write b equals a. You change b, and a changes too. No error, just wrong data. The fix is the copy method. B equals a dot copy. Now b is its own list, and a stays exactly as it was. Always ask yourself, do I need a second name, or a second list? Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Name or copy?

shorts.hook: "Why did the two names get along so well?"
shorts.script: Why did the two names get along so well? They were pointing at the same thing. Your challenge. Make a list a, with ten, twenty, thirty. Make a real copy called b. Append forty to b only. Then print both lists. Check that a still has three items, and b has four. Post your result in the comments, please. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 28.
